title: NULLIF has the type of its first argument, whichever common type it compares in
verdict: `NULLIF(a, b)` is typed as `a`, though it compares in the common type; the lift types it as the common type
description: `NULLIF(1::INTEGER, 1.5::DOUBLE)` is an INTEGER, `NULLIF(1::BIGINT, 1::INTEGER)` a BIGINT and `NULLIF(1::INTEGER, 1::BIGINT)` an INTEGER. The comparison runs in the common type; the result keeps the first argument's, so `NULLIF(1::INTEGER, 1.5::DOUBLE) + 9223372036854775807::BIGINT` raises `Overflow in addition of INT64`.
reference: The lift's `_nullif` (`sql_lift/core.py`) casts both arguments to `common` and types the result with it: `NULLIF(i32, f64)` is a float64 in the plan, `NULLIF(i32, i64)` an int64. The value is the same; the type is not, so arithmetic on the result differs (a double sum where DuckDB raises an integer overflow, a 64-bit sum where DuckDB's is 32-bit). The plan should compare in the common type and cast the result back to the first argument's type.

evidence.note: `nullif` is the macro `CASE WHEN a=b THEN NULL ELSE a END`: the comparison binds in the common type, the result is `a`
